candidates.attacker_control: A remote, unauthenticated client controls the multipart request body: field name, number of parts, each part's body length, and the transfer framing. A single form field (Content-Disposition without a filename, so `part.getSubmittedFileName() == null`) larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE triggers the narrowing-cast wrap; alternatively many parts can drive the cumulative `int` total past Integer.MAX_VALUE.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the maxPostSize guard really is the only limiter on non-file part size: FileUpload is configured with mce limits (unlimited by default for @MultipartConfig), `fileCountMax` only bounds part count, and the postSize check is the sole size gate before `part.getString()`. Verified the guard is not duplicated elsewhere for this path. Checked the casual-multipart path (mce == null): there sizeMax is set to connector maxPostSize, so the single-part wrap requires an explicitly configured MultipartConfigElement (common) or a large configured limit for the cumulative variant. Confirmed `part.getSize()` and `ApplicationPart.getSize()` are `long`, and `DiskFileItem.getString()` does `new String(get(), charset)` (full in-memory materialization). Checked that the cast/overflow happens before the comparison, i.e., the limit cannot catch the wrapped value. Could not diff against upstream or run code to confirm which release fixed it.
candidates.impact: Bypass of the container's maxPostSize resource limit on multipart (and chunked form POST) processing, resulting in attacker-controlled unbounded heap consumption and Denial of Service (OutOfMemoryError, GC pressure, possible loss of the whole Tomcat process). No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed; the defect is a resource-exhaustion/limit-bypass issue.
candidates.prerequisites: The request must be routed to a servlet with an effective `@MultipartConfig`/`MultipartConfigElement` (the standard case for upload endpoints). The annotation defaults are maxFileSize=-1 and maxRequestSize=-1 (unlimited) with fileSizeThreshold=0, so a >2 GiB part is accepted by the bundled FileUpload parser. The attacker must be able to send a body/part of more than 2 GiB (chunked or with Content-Length); no credentials are inherently required. When `@MultipartConfig` limits are explicitly set below 2 GiB the single-part wrap is not reachable, but large configured limits still allow the cumulative variant.
candidates.root_cause: In `org.apache.catalina.connector.Request.parseParts()` the equivalent POST size for non-file multipart parts is accumulated in a 32-bit `int postSize` (line 2505) and each part's length is added through a narrowing cast `(int) part.getSize()` (line 2519). A single non-file part whose size exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647 bytes) wraps to a negative value when cast, so the running total goes negative and the guard `if (postSize > maxPostSize)` at line 2522 never fires. Execution then continues to `part.getString(charset.name())` (line 2528), which materializes the whole part in heap memory. The intended connector-level `maxPostSize` limit (2 MiB by default) is therefore not enforced. `Request.readChunkedPostBody()` (line 2932) uses the same 32-bit expression `body.getLength() + len` to enforce the same limit, so the same wrap-around class exists on that path.
candidates.title: Integer overflow in multipart request-size accounting bypasses maxPostSize and enables memory-exhaustion DoS
candidates.trace: 1) Request with `Content-Type: multipart/form-data` reaches `Request.doParseParameters()` and then `parseParts()` (Request.java:2425). 2) `upload.setFileSizeMax(mce.getMaxFileSize())` / `upload.setSizeMax(mce.getMaxRequestSize())` are -1 by default, so the parser accepts an arbitrarily large part (Request.java:2491-2492); `upload.parseRequest` stores the part on disk via DiskFileItem. 3) In the loop over parsed items, for a part without a submitted filename the code executes `postSize += (int) part.getSize()` (Request.java:2519); for part size > Integer.MAX_VALUE the cast result is negative, so `postSize` becomes negative and `postSize > maxPostSize` (line 2522) is false. 4) The code proceeds to `part.getString(charset.name())` (line 2528) -> `DiskFileItem.getString()` -> `new String(get(), charset)`, which reads the entire >2 GiB part into a byte[] plus String. 5) The result is a very large heap allocation / OutOfMemoryError (or repeated large allocations under concurrency) although the configured maxPostSize should have rejected the request. The analogous comparison in `readChunkedPostBody()` (line 2932) uses the same 32-bit sum before the size check.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. The snapshot was not diffed against upstream/patched revisions, so it is not proven that this exact expression is the code changed by the corresponding fix; the mapping to a specific CVE (e.g., a 2025 Tomcat multipart DoS advisory) is inferred from the 11.0.8-dev snapshot date and the code shape. Exploitability depends on the deployed servlet's MultipartConfig limits and on the attacker's ability to transfer >2 GiB; the chunked-POST variant additionally depends on a large maxPostSize.
candidates.weakness_type: Integer Overflow or Wraparound (CWE-190) leading to resource-exhaustion Denial of Service (CWE-400/CWE-770)

coverage_summary: Scope: 2,977 repository-visible text files under the assigned root (binary-like files skipped by the reader/search policy; no test tree or git metadata is visible in this snapshot). Version markers indicate Apache Tomcat 11.0.8-dev circa June 2025. I read/targeted-searched the request-processing core (org.apache.catalina.connector.CoyoteAdapter/Request/Connector, org.apache.coyote.http11, org.apache.coyote.http2, org.apache.tomcat.util.http.* and .http.parser.*), the bundled fileupload fork (FileUploadBase, MultipartStream, FileItemIteratorImpl, FileItemStreamImpl, DiskFileItem, Streams), request/response and parameter handling (Parameters, MimeHeaders, UDecoder), web resource and servlet paths (AbstractFileResourceSet, DirResourceSet, DefaultServlet, WebdavServlet), rewrite valve, authenticators/session handling, and manager webapp JSPs, plus repo-level docs/changelog and build/CI metadata. Patterns searched included process execution APIs, trust/hostname verification, MD5/Random usage, part/parameter size limits, suspicious-URI checks, and file-count/header-size limits. Coverage is broad but not exhaustive; the strongest lead is in Request.parseParts().
limitations: No tests, build outputs, or git history/patch data are present in the visible snapshot, so the code could not be diffed against upstream or the fixing revision, and no runtime/exploit validation was performed (and was out of scope).

Binary-like files and any symlinks/filters described by get_source_scope were skipped; areas not read line-by-line (e.g., JSP/Jasper compiler internals, tribes/cluster, naming/JNDI, JDBC/DBCP realms, WebSocket internals, JASPIC) were only searched at a high level.

The exact CVE/version mapping and the severity/exploitability of the candidate are inferred from source shape, documentation defaults, and the snapshot date; the >2 GiB transfer requirement and dependence on the application's MultipartConfig make practical impact configuration-dependent.
Alternative leads (suspicious-URI encoded-control threshold `decoded < 20`, uncounted skipped multipart parts) remain unverified and could also be latent defects.

rejected_leads.lead: CoyoteAdapter.checkSuspiciousURIs() rejects encoded control characters with the test `decoded < 20` (decimal 20 = 0x14) instead of `decoded < 0x20` (line 1288), so %-encoded control characters 0x14-0x1F are not classified as suspicious. Since the connector attribute `rejectSuspiciousURIs` defaults to false and the code also catches invalid hex values via the negative return of HexUtils.getDec, the practical security effect is limited to opt-in deployments. Style anomaly may be an upstream quirk; no matching CVE could be established from source alone.
rejected_leads.reason: Real but low-impact/opt-in hardening gap; cannot confirm it deviates from upstream, so it is not the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: In FileUploadBase/FileItemIteratorImpl, `fileCountMax` is checked in FileUploadBase.parseRequest() against the number of items returned by the iterator; parts that never produce a FileItemStream (Content-Disposition without a `name`, or inner multipart/mixed parts without a filename) are silently skipped in FileItemIteratorImpl.findNextItem() and are not counted. A multipart body can therefore contain an unbounded number of skipped parts (bounded only by request-size configuration and socket time).
rejected_leads.reason: Impact is CPU/bandwidth-bound parsing rather than accumulation of memory or files; requires a multipart-enabled endpoint and large configured request limits. Weaker exploitability and impact than the integer-overflow candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: HTTP/2 DoS surface (overhead counting in Http2UpgradeHandler, stream pruning, HPACK/header-size enforcement, unknown-frame handling) was inspected for missing limits; the parsing and stream-lifetime paths looked self-consistent (overhead counted for SETTINGS/PING/RST/PRIORITY_UPDATE/HEADERS/DATA/WINDOW_UPDATE, streams pruned to 5x maxConcurrentStreams, header count/size enforced via Http2Protocol).
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete source-level defect identified; remaining suspicion is speculative.

rejected_leads.lead: WebDAV Destination handling, DefaultServlet partial-PUT range validation, DirResourceSet/AbstractFileResourceSet path canonicalization, FormAuthenticator saved requests, rewrite-valve URI re-encoding/normalization, and manager JSP escaping were reviewed and no clear exploitable defect was found in this snapshot.
rejected_leads.reason: No source evidence of a vulnerability beyond the checked hardening patterns; not submitted to respect the one-candidate limit.

summary: The snapshot is an Apache Tomcat 11.0.8-dev tree (changelog top section "Tomcat 11.0.8 (markt) in development"; MERGE.txt records a Commons FileUpload fork commit dated 2025-06-05). I reviewed the externally reachable request-processing paths (CoyoteAdapter URI handling, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 parsers, Request/Parameters, multipart/FileUpload fork, RewriteValve, DefaultServlet/WebdavServlet, web resource path checks, manager webapp escaping) and searched for common weakness patterns. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is a 32-bit integer overflow in the multipart request-size accounting inside Request.parseParts(): a part larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE makes the `(int) part.getSize()` cast wrap negative, so the maxPostSize guard cannot fire and the part is subsequently read fully into memory, defeating the intended resource limit (DoS). The same 32-bit accounting pattern exists in Request.readChunkedPostBody(). Other suspicious areas were inspected but are weaker or unconfirmed and are listed as rejected leads.
